en: Thus have I heard— Majjhima Nikāya 102, the Discourse on the Fivefold Set (Pañcattayasutta).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, there are certain recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the future, who hold views regarding the future, and who assert various kinds of propositions concerning the future.”
‘The self is percipient and unimpaired after death’—
thus some assert;
‘The self is non-percipient and unimpaired after death’— thus some assert.
In this regard, some assert:
"The self is neither percipient nor non-percipient and is healthy after death"—
thus some assert.
Or they proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being; or some assert Nibbāna in this very life.

Thus, they either proclaim a self that exists and is healthy after death, or they proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being; or some assert Nibbāna in this very life.
Thus, these five become three, and these three become five.
This is the summary of the fivefold triad.
In this regard, monks, those recluses and brahmins who describe the self as percipient and healthy after death—
those venerable recluses and brahmins describe the self as percipient and healthy after death as either possessing form, or...
Or those worthy recluses and brahmins describe the self as percipient and formless, healthy after death;
or those worthy recluses and brahmins describe the self as percipient and both with form and formless, healthy after death;
or those worthy recluses and brahmins describe the self as percipient and neither with form nor formless, healthy after death.

After death, those venerable recluses and brahmins describe the self as percipient and healthy after death, either as having a single mode of perception, or as having diverse modes of perception, or as having limited perception.
"Or else, those venerable recluses and brahmins describe the self as percipient and healthy after death;
or they describe it as having immeasurable perception and healthy after death; or, for some who have transcended this, they assert a kasiṇa of consciousness that is immeasurable and imperturbable.
This, monks, the Tathāgata directly knows."
Those worthy recluses and brahmins who describe the self as percipient and healthy after death—
those worthy recluses and brahmins describe that self as percipient and healthy after death as either possessing form, or as formless, or as both possessing form and...
Or those worthy recluses and brahmins describe the self as percipient and formless, healthy after death;
or those worthy recluses and brahmins describe the self as percipient and neither-form-nor-formless, healthy after death;
or those worthy recluses and brahmins describe the self as percipient and possessing a singular perception, healthy after death.

After death, those venerable recluses and brahmins describe the self as percipient and healthy after death, either as having diverse perceptions, or as having limited perceptions, or as having immeasurable perceptions.
Health beyond death, or whatever among these perceptions is declared to be purified, supreme, foremost, and unsurpassed— whether it be perceptions of form,
perceptions of the formless, perceptions of unity, or perceptions of diversity— or the base of nothingness,
which some proclaim as "there is nothing," being immeasurable and imperturbable.
‘This is conditioned and gross; however, there is a cessation of formations, and that exists’—having understood this, the Tathāgata, seeing its escape, has transcended it.
In this regard, bhikkhus, those recluses and brahmins who describe the self as non-percipient and healthy beyond death—
Or those worthy recluses and brahmins describe the self as having form and non-percipient, healthy after death;
or those worthy recluses and brahmins describe the self as formless and non-percipient, healthy after death;
or those worthy recluses and brahmins describe the self as both having form and being formless and non-percipient, healthy after death.
After death, those venerable recluses and brahmins who describe the self as neither material nor immaterial,
but percipient and healthy after death—
against them, monks, those recluses and brahmins who describe the self as percipient and healthy after death raise their objections.
For what reason?
Perception is a disease, perception is a tumor, perception is a dart; this is peaceful, this is sublime, namely: ‘non-perception.
This, monks, the Tathāgata directly knows.
Those venerable recluses and brahmins who describe the self as non-percipient and healthy after death—
those venerable recluses and brahmins describe the self as non-percipient and healthy after death as either possessing form, or as being formless, or as both possessing form and [being formless].
Or those worthy recluses and brahmins describe the self as formless and non-percipient, healthy after death;
or those worthy recluses and brahmins describe the self as neither-form-nor-formless and non-percipient, healthy after death.
For whatever recluse or brahmin, monks, might say this:

‘Apart from form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, apart from volitional formations, I shall describe the coming or going, the passing away or rebirth, the growth, increase, or fullness of consciousness’—this is impossible.
‘This is conditioned and gross; however, there is the cessation of volitional formations, and that exists.’”
Having understood this, the Tathāgata—who sees the escape from it—has transcended that state.
In this regard, monks, those ascetics and brahmins who describe the self as being neither percipient nor non-percipient and healthy beyond death:
do those worthy ascetics and brahmins describe the self as being neither percipient nor non-percipient and possessing form?
Those worthy recluses and brahmins describe the self as neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient after death as healthy and formless;
or those worthy recluses and brahmins describe the self as neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient after death as both healthy and both form and formless;
or those worthy recluses and brahmins [describe it] as neither form nor formless... after death as healthy.
They describe the self as neither percipient nor non-percipient and healthy after death.
In this regard, monks, those recluses and brahmins who describe the self as percipient and healthy after death they refute;
and those venerable recluses and brahmins who describe the self as non-percipient and healthy... [they also refute].
After death, they reject these very things. And why is that?
Perception is a disease, perception is a tumor, perception is a dart; non-perception is delusion. This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely: [the state of non-perception].
‘Neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Monks, the Tathāgata directly knows this.
Those venerable recluses and brahmins who describe the self as being neither percipient nor non-percipient, healthy, and beyond [death]—[the Tathāgata knows them].
After death, those venerable recluses and brahmins describe the self as having form and neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, healthy after death;
or those venerable recluses and brahmins describe the self as being formless and neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, healthy after death;
or those venerable recluses and brahmins [describe it] as both having form and being formless and neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient... after death.

They describe the self as healthy after death, neither possessing form nor being formless; those venerable recluses and brahmins describe the self as neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, healthy after death.
For whatever recluses or brahmins there may be, bhikkhus, who [describe the self] by means of the mere conditioned phenomena that are seen, heard, sensed, or cognized—
They prescribe the full admission to this sphere, but, monks, it is declared that such full admission to this sphere leads to ruin. For this sphere,
monks, is not declared to be attainable through the attainment of conditioned formations.
“Monks, this base is declared to be that which is to be attained through the attainment of the remainder of volitional formations.
Having understood: ‘This is conditioned and gross; however, there is the cessation of volitional formations, and this exists,’ the Tathāgata, seeing the escape from it, has transcended it.”
In this regard, monks, those recluses and brahmins who proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being—
therein, monks, they refute those recluses and brahmins who proclaim a conscious self that is healthy after death;
and they also refute those venerable recluses and brahmins who proclaim an unconscious self that is healthy [after death].
They refute those venerable recluses and brahmins who describe the self as neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient and healthy after death;
they refute them for this reason. And why is that?
All these worthy recluses and brahmins, however, profess attachment to a future existence, saying:
"Thus we shall become after death; thus we shall become after death.
It is just as if a merchant, while going on business, thinks to himself: [and so forth].
‘From this, this will be mine; by means of this, I shall obtain that.
In just this way, these venerable recluses and brahmins appear to me like merchants:
‘Thus we shall become after passing away; thus we shall become after passing away.’
“Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata understands this:

‘Those venerable recluses and brahmins who proclaim the annihilation, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being do so because they fear identity-view (sakkāya), loathe identity-view, and thus run and circle around that very identity-view.
It is just as if a dog were tied with a leash to a strong post or stake; it would simply run and circle around that same post or stake.”
In the same way, these worthy recluses and brahmins, out of fear of self-identity and loathing of self-identity, run and circle around nothing but self-identity itself.
But the Tathāgata, having understood: "This is conditioned and gross; however, there is a cessation of formations, and that exists," and seeing the escape from it, has transcended it.
"Whatever recluses or brahmins, bhikkhus, who are speculators about the future, holding views regarding the future,
and who assert various descriptions concerning the future— all of them assert these very five bases,
or one or another of them."
“Bhikkhus, there are some recluses and brahmins who are speculators about the past, who hold views regarding the past, and who assert various doctrinal propositions concerning the past.
Some assert: ‘The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
Others assert: ‘The self and the world are non-eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.’”
In this regard, some assert: “The self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal; this alone is true, all else is false. In this regard, some assert:
“The self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
In this regard, some assert: “The self and the world are finite; this alone is true, all else is false.”
In this regard, some assert: "The self and the world are infinite; this alone is true, all else is false. Some assert:
"The self and the world are both finite and infinite; this alone is true, all else is false. Some assert:
"The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite; this alone is true, all else is false."
In this regard, some assert: "The self and the world are percipient of unity; only this is true, all else is false. In this regard, some assert:
"The self and the world are percipient of diversity; only this is true, all else is false. In this regard, some assert:
"The self and the world are percipient of the limited; only this is true, all else is false."
In this regard, some assert: "The self and the world are infinite in perception; only this is true, all else is false. In this regard, some assert:
"The self and the world are exclusively happy; only this is true, all else is false. In this regard, some assert:
"The self and the world are exclusively suffering; only this is true, all else is false."
In this regard, some assert: "The self and the world experience both pleasure and pain; this alone is true, all else is false.
In this regard, some assert: "The self and the world experience neither-pain-nor-pleasure; this alone is true, all else is false. Thus do some assert.
In this regard, monks, as for those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as:

“The self and the world are eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is vain”—surely their [conviction] is apart from faith, apart from personal preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection on modes, and apart from acceptance based on the contemplation of views.
"It is impossible that there will be a knowledge within oneself that is purified and cleansed— this cannot be.
But, monks, when there is no such purified and cleansed knowledge within oneself,
even that mere portion of knowledge which those venerable recluses and brahmins cleanse in that regard is declared to be clinging on the part of those venerable recluses and brahmins."
‘This is conditioned and gross, but there is indeed a cessation of formations; this exists.
Having understood this, the Tathāgata—who sees the escape from it—has transcended that.
In this regard, bhikkhus, those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:

‘The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false’ … ‘The self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal’ … ‘The self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal’ … [and so forth].
The self and the world are finite… the self and the world are infinite… the self and the world are both finite and infinite…
Neither finite nor infinite is the self and the world … perceiving unity,
the self and the world … perceiving diversity, the self and the world …
The self and the world are perceived as limited...
the self and the world are perceived as immeasurable...
the self and the world are exclusively happy...
“The self and the world are exclusively subject to suffering… the self and the world are subject to both pleasure and pain… the self and the world are subject to neither-pain-nor-pleasure;
this alone is true, all else is false”— for them, indeed, apart from this very [view]...

"It is impossible that there will be a personal knowledge, pure and bright, apart from conviction, apart from preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from the acceptance of a view after pondering it—
this cannot be. But when there is no personal knowledge, bhikkhus, that is pure and bright, then even those venerable ones..."
Therein, those ascetics and brahmins merely purify a portion of knowledge; yet even that is declared to be clinging on the part of those venerable ascetics and brahmins. Having understood:
"This is conditioned, gross, but there is indeed the cessation of formations;
this exists," the Tathāgata, seeing the escape from it, has transcended it.
In this case, monks, a certain ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views concerning the past and the relinquishing of views concerning the future,
and by not adhering at all to the fetters of sensual desire,
enters and dwells in the rapture of seclusion:
‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, that I dwell having attained the rapture of seclusion.
His rapture of seclusion ceases.
With the cessation of the rapture of seclusion, grief arises; with the cessation of grief, the rapture of seclusion arises.
“Just as, monks, where shade leaves, there heat pervades, and where heat leaves, there shade pervades;
even so, monks, with the cessation of the rapture of seclusion, dejection arises, and with the cessation of dejection, the rapture of seclusion arises.
This, monks, the Tathāgata understands.”
This venerable ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views concerning the past and the relinquishing of views concerning the future,
and through the total non-adherence to the fetters of sensual desire, dwells having attained the rapture of seclusion,
thinking: "This is peaceful, this is sublime, that I dwell having attained the rapture of seclusion."
His rapture of seclusion ceases.
With the cessation of the rapture of seclusion, grief arises; with the cessation of grief, the rapture of seclusion arises.
"This is conditioned and gross, yet there is indeed a cessation of formations; this exists"—[he understands this].
Having understood this, the Tathāgata— who sees the escape from it—
has transcended it. Furthermore, monks, here a certain ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views concerning the past and the relinquishing of views concerning the future,
and through the total non-adherence to the fetters of sensual desire, [abides] for the sake of seclusion.
With the surmounting of rapture, he dwells having attained spiritual happiness, thinking:
"This is peaceful, this is sublime, that I dwell having attained spiritual happiness.
That spiritual happiness of his ceases.
With the cessation of unworldly happiness, the rapture of seclusion arises; with the cessation of the rapture of seclusion, unworldly happiness arises.
Just as, monks, where the shade leaves, there the sunlight pervades, and where the sunlight leaves, there the shade pervades;
even so, monks, with the cessation of unworldly happiness, the rapture of seclusion arises, and with the cessation of the rapture of seclusion, unworldly happiness arises.
This, monks, the Tathāgata directly knows.
This venerable ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views concerning the past and the relinquishing of views concerning the future,
through the complete non-adherence to the fetters of sensual desire, and through the surmounting of the rapture of seclusion—
He dwells having attained spiritual happiness, thinking:
"This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, that I dwell having attained spiritual happiness.
Yet, that spiritual happiness of his ceases.
With the cessation of unworldly happiness, the rapture of seclusion arises; with the cessation of the rapture of seclusion, unworldly happiness arises.
Having understood: "This is conditioned and gross, but there is indeed a cessation of formations;
this exists," the Tathāgata, seeing the escape from it, has transcended it.
But here, monks, a certain ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views concerning the past and the relinquishing of views concerning the future,
by not adhering in any way to the fetters of sensual desire, by transcending the rapture of seclusion,
and by transcending unworldly pleasure, dwells having attained the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant:
‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, that I dwell having attained the feeling that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Then that neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling of his ceases.
With the cessation of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, non-sensual pleasure arises; with the cessation of non-sensual pleasure, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.
“Just as, monks, where the shadow leaves, there the sunlight pervades, and where the sunlight leaves, there the shadow pervades;
even so, monks, with the cessation of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unworldly happiness arises, and with the cessation of unworldly happiness, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.
This, monks, the Tathāgata directly knows.”
This venerable ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views regarding the past and the relinquishing of views regarding the future,
through the total non-adherence to the fetters of sensual desire, through the surmounting of the rapture of seclusion,
and through the surmounting of unworldly pleasure, dwells having attained the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant:
‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, that I enter and dwell in this feeling which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
That neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling of his ceases.
With the cessation of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, non-sensual pleasure arises; with the cessation of the non-sensual pleasure, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.
‘This is conditioned and gross; however, there is indeed a cessation of formations, and that exists.
Having understood this, the Tathāgata—who sees the escape from it—has transcended it.
But here, monks, a certain ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views regarding the past...

Through the relinquishing of views concerning the future, through the complete non-adherence to the fetters of sensual desire, through the surmounting of the rapture of seclusion, through the surmounting of unworldly pleasure, and through the surmounting of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one regards oneself thus:
"I am at peace; I am extinguished; I am without clinging."
This, monks, the Tathāgata directly knows:
"This venerable ascetic or brahmin, through the relinquishing of views concerning the past and the relinquishing of views concerning the future,
through the complete non-adherence to the fetters of sensual desire, and through the surmounting of the rapture of seclusion..."
Having transcended unworldly happiness and having transcended neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he regards himself thus:
"I am at peace, I am extinguished, I am without clinging.
Surely this venerable one approves of a practice that is truly conducive to Nibbāna.
And yet, this venerable ascetic or brahmin, while grasping, grasps at a view concerning the past;
or while grasping, he grasps at a view concerning the future; or while grasping, he grasps at the fetter of sensual desire;
or while grasping, he grasps at the rapture of seclusion; or while grasping, he grasps at unworldly happiness.
Or, when grasping at a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, one grasps it.
Furthermore, when this venerable one regards himself thus:
"I am at peace, I am extinguished, I am without grasping," even that is declared to be grasping for this worthy ascetic or brahmin.
‘This is conditioned and gross; however, there is indeed a cessation of formations, and that exists’—having understood this, the Tathāgata, seeing its escape, has transcended it.
And this, monks, is the unsurpassed supreme state of peace awakened to by the Tathāgata, namely: [the cessation of formations].
"Having understood, as they really are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact, there is liberation through non-clinging.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
With uplifted minds, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Discourse on the Five Bases is finished; this is the second.
